utterances.text: Hey! Good morning. How are you doing today?
Oh, hey. I'm doing well, thanks. Just getting settled in.
How about you?
I'm good, yeah. Just had some coffee, so I'm ready to go.
How was your weekend?
Did you get a chance to do anything fun?
It was pretty quiet, actually.
I mostly just stayed in and caught up on some reading.
You know, just trying to relax a bit before the week kicks off.
It was nice to have some downtime.
Yeah, I totally get that.
Sometimes you just need to zone out for a bit.
Did you do anything else, or was it mostly just a chill one?
A bit of both.
I did go out for a walk on Sunday afternoon, which was nice.
The weather was actually decent for once, so I just wandered around the neighborhood for a while.
It was refreshing.
Oh, that sounds great.
The weather has been a bit unpredictable lately, so catching a nice day is always a win.
I actually spent most of mine just catching up on some chores and then finally watched that show everyone's been talking about.
Oh, the one on Netflix?
Yeah, that's the one. It was... honestly, it was pretty good.
I ended up binge-watching a few episodes in one sitting.
I should probably have more self-control, but, you know, it was a good way to unwind.
Right? It's so easy to just fall into those.
I do that all the time.
Anyway, how are you feeling about the week ahead?
You seem like you're in a good headspace.
I'm feeling good.
A little bit of the usual Monday morning fog, but I'm feeling motivated.
There's a lot on the plate, but I think we're in a good spot with the current sprint.
I'm looking forward to getting some of those blockers cleared out.
Mm-hmm. That's good to hear.
I know things have been a bit hectic with the latest updates, but I appreciate you keeping the team focused.
Yeah, for sure.
It's been a bit of a push, but the team is really stepping up.
They're... they're doing a great job handling the pivots.
They really are. Anyway, I'm glad you're feeling positive about it.
Let's dive into the first item on the agenda then.
Sounds good. Let's do it.
So, moving on to the team pulse...
how are you feeling about the general vibe this week?
I mean, from your perspective, watching them in the stand-ups and the Slack channels.
Um, honestly? It’s a bit of a mixed bag.
I mean, the energy is there, but it feels...
I don't know, a bit strained?
Like they're pushing hard, but maybe a bit too hard on the sprint goals.
Right. Strain is different from just being busy.
Do you think it's the workload or is it something more specific?
I think it's a bit of both, I guess.
There's this specific bottleneck with the integration layer that's just...
it's been dragging on.
And I can see it starting to wear on the devs.
They're getting a bit frustrated with the constant back-and-forth.
Yeah, I've noticed that too.
I saw a few long threads in the dev channel yesterday.
People are getting a bit... well, they're getting a bit snappy.
It's not a huge deal, but it's noticeable.
Exactly.
And I'm worried that if we don't address the frustration, it's going to start affecting the morale for the next cycle.
Like, they're starting to feel like they're spinning their wheels.
Mm-hmm. That's the thing I want to watch out for.
I don't want them feeling like they're just grinding for the sake of grinding.
I think we might need to...
uh, maybe pull back a little on the non-essential tasks for the next week?
Just to give them some breathing room.
That might be a good idea.
Just a little bit of a breather.
They need to feel like they're actually crossing things off the list, you know?
Right.
Because when they feel like they're stuck in a loop, that's when the burnout starts to creep in.
I'll try to...
I'll try to keep an eye on the tone in the meetings.
I can try to redirect some of the frustration into, I don't know, more collaborative problem-solving instead of just venting.
Yeah, that would be great. Just keep it positive.
They really look up to you for the...
the technical direction, but they also look to you to see how they should be feeling about the project.
Yeah, I get that. I'll make sure to...
uh, I'll make sure to keep the focus on the wins we're actually getting.
Even the small ones. It helps a lot with the morale.
Good. Let's just keep an eye on it.
If it gets worse, we'll have to...
we'll have to have a bigger talk about the roadmap.
Yeah. Definitely. Let's just keep it on the radar.
So, moving on to the Atlas project, I wanted to give you a quick update on where we are with the beta phase.
Specifically, the sign-ups and the general readiness of the platform.
Yeah, that's a big one.
I've been getting some questions from the marketing side about how many people are actually in the system right now.
Right.
Well, we have 38 customers signed up for the beta so far.
Okay. Is that... is that what we were expecting at this stage?
Um, it's a bit lower than the initial goal we set, but, uh, the quality of the feedback from those thirty-eight is actually really high.
They're engaging with the core features, and we're getting some very specific notes on the UI.
I see. So the numbers aren't perfect, but the engagement is there?
Exactly.
And, well, the reason the numbers are a bit lower is because we've been a bit more selective with the invite list to ensure we're only getting users who can give us constructive feedback.
We don't want to overwhelm the dev team with noise from people who aren't really the target audience.
That makes sense.
I guess it's better to have a smaller, focused group.
Yeah, definitely. Now, regarding the readiness... the core infrastructure is stable.
We've cleared the major bugs from the last sprint, and the deployment pipeline is, uh, it's much smoother now.
We're feeling confident about the stability.
Good. And what about the... the secondary features?
The ones we were going to push back if we hit roadblocks?
Oh, those are mostly ready.
We had a bit of a hiccup with the notification system, but we managed to patch that last week.
So, in terms of readiness, I'd say we're about, um, ninety percent there for the public launch.
We just need to polish a few minor things in the reporting module.
Okay.
So, if we stay on this track, do you think we're ready for the next phase?
I believe so.
If we can just get those final tweaks done, we're in a very good position.
The team is feeling good about it, honestly.
They're excited to see it go live.
That's good to hear.
I'll tell the stakeholders that the progress is steady.
Yeah, that would be great.
I can send over a summary of those specific points if that helps you with your next meeting.
Yeah, that would be perfect. Thanks.
So, yeah, looking at the current sprint, the main thing holding us back from the Atlas beta is really just that final integration with the notification engine.
It's...
it's mostly stable, but we're seeing some intermittent lag when the volume spikes.
Right.
And is that a known issue with the third-party API or is that something internal?
It's a bit of both, honestly.
We're trying to optimize the way we call the endpoint to reduce the overhead.
It's not a showstopper, but we want it to be smooth for the first batch of users.
We don't want them getting stuck in a loading state.
I understand. We definitely want a polished experience for the launch.
If we don't fix that, it'll be a headache for support immediately.
Exactly. And then there's the documentation.
The team is still polishing the help guides.
We want to make sure that when people sign up, they actually know how to navigate the dashboard without having to email us every five minutes.
That makes sense.
I'd rather we take a little extra time on the docs than have a messy rollout.
Yeah, I agree.
We're also just double-checking the edge cases for the user permissions.
It's a lot of moving parts, but we're getting there.
We just need a bit of breathing room to hammer out those final bugs.
Okay, let's lock it in: the Atlas beta moves to March 3.
Yes, March 3 works for us.
Good.
That gives us a solid window to get those final checks done without feeling like we're rushing the finish line.
Mm-hmm. That's a good buffer.
It allows the dev team to focus on the stability of the notification system without the pressure of a looming deadline that's too tight.
It gives us a bit of...
uh, a bit of breathing room to just get it right.
Right. I think that's the best move for the team's morale too.
They're working hard, and we don't want them burning out in the final week.
Yeah, definitely.
They're feeling good about the progress, just want to make sure the launch is smooth.
So, moving on to the feedback from the early testers...
I've been going through the logs and the survey responses from the first group that got in.
Yeah, I've been looking forward to hearing that. What's the general vibe?
It's... well, it's mostly positive, but there are some specific pain points.
They really love the core functionality, the way the dashboard handles the data visualization is getting a lot of praise.
They said it's intuitive.
That's good. That's what we were hoping for with the UI overhaul.
Right, exactly.
But, um, there are some complaints about the loading times on the reporting module.
It seems like it's hanging for a few seconds too long when they try to export.
Is that a backend issue or something with the front-end rendering?
It's a bit of both, honestly.
The query is taking longer than expected because of the volume of data, and then the front-end is struggling to process the results.
So, we need to optimize the query first before we can really fix the UI lag.
Okay. And anything else? Anything else specific?
Yeah, a few people mentioned that the notification system is a bit...
well, it's a bit noisy.
They're getting alerts for things they don't really need to see in real-time.
They want more granular controls over what triggers a notification.
Mm-hmm. That makes sense.
We should probably add some toggle switches for those.
Exactly. And, uh, one more thing.
One tester pointed out that the mobile view for the settings page is slightly broken.
The buttons are overlapping.
It's not a dealbreaker, but it's something we should probably polish before the wider rollout.
Okay, so we have the loading times, the notification logic, and the mobile CSS.
Is that everything from the first batch?
Mostly.
There was one request for a dark mode, but we agreed to put that on the roadmap for later.
We need to stay focused on the core stability for now.
Right, right. Focus on the essentials.
Yeah.
I'll have the team prioritize the reporting speed first since that's the biggest friction point for the power users.
Good. Let's do that.
So, moving into the actual risks...
I've been chatting with the devs and the QA folks, and there are two main things that keep coming up as the biggest hurdles for the beta launch.
Okay, I'm interested to hear what they're saying.
Is it mostly technical stuff?
It's a mix.
The first one, and honestly the one that keeps me up a bit, is the scalability of the notification engine.
Right now, it works perfectly for a few hundred users, but if we hit a spike—like, if the marketing push actually works—the system might just...
well, it might choke.
It's not that it won't work, it's just that the current architecture isn't built for a massive surge in real-time pings.
That makes sense.
We don't want a surge to crash the whole experience.
Exactly.
To mitigate that, the team is proposing a phased rollout for the notifications.
Instead of everyone getting everything at once, we'd stagger the rollout by region or by user group.
It gives us a buffer to monitor the load and scale the infrastructure incrementally rather than trying to handle a massive wave all at once.
Mm-hmm. And the second one?
The second one is more about the data integrity during the migration of the legacy profiles.
Because we're moving some of the older data structures into the new schema, there's a risk of some fields getting...
well, they might get dropped or mapped incorrectly.
It's a bit of a headache because we can't just have users logging in and seeing blank profiles.
Right, that would be a huge pain for the early adopters.
Yeah, exactly.
So, the plan there is to run a series of 'shadow' migrations.
Basically, we run the migration in a staging environment that mirrors the production data exactly, and we do this multiple times before we actually flip the switch.
We want to catch those edge cases where a specific type of user profile might break the script.
We're also building a manual override tool just in case we need to fix a specific account quickly without having to roll back the whole migration.
Okay.
So, so if we do those two things, do you feel more confident about the launch?
I mean, it's not a guarantee, but it significantly lowers the probability of a catastrophic failure.
If we handle the notification load gracefully and we're 100% sure on the data mapping, the team feels much more comfortable.
It moves the risk from 'it might break everything' to 'we have a plan if things get heavy'.
I like that distinction. Let's stick with that plan.
Yeah, I'll have the team document those specific mitigation steps in the sprint plan so we can track the progress on the shadow migrations specifically.
Yeah, so, looking at the roadmap for the next few months, the biggest bottleneck we're hitting right now is definitely the back-end processing.
The team is feeling a bit stretched trying to juggle the Atlas features while also trying to keep the current data flows stable.
I know, I've heard that from a few of the others too.
It's a lot of manual heavy lifting right now.
Exactly.
And if we want to scale the beta without the system crashing every time we get a spike in traffic, we really need to automate those ingestion points.
It's becoming a bit of a headache for the engineers to keep patching it manually.
Good news, I got approval for two contractors for the data pipeline.
Oh, that's... um, that's huge.
That's actually exactly what we need right now.
Having dedicated hands just for the pipeline stuff would let the core team focus on the actual product features.
Right, it should take some of the pressure off the sprint cycles.
Yeah, definitely. So, in terms of how we onboard them...
I was thinking we could have them start on the legacy migration first?
Because that's the messiest part of the code right now.
If they can clean that up, it makes everything else much easier.
That makes sense.
Do you think they'll need a lot of oversight from you initially?
Well, uh, for the first couple of weeks, probably.
I'll need to sit down with them to map out the architecture, but once they get the hang of the environment, they should be able to run with it.
I don't want to pull the senior devs away from the Atlas work for too much, so the goal is to get these contractors up to speed as fast as possible.
Okay. And what about the documentation?
Is that sufficient for someone coming in from the outside?
It's... it's okay. I mean, it's functional, but it's not great.
I'll probably have to spend some time, maybe a few afternoons, just getting them up to speed on the specific quirks of our database.
But honestly, having two people on it is going to be a game changer.
It's a huge relief.
I'm glad to hear that.
It's a big win for the team's morale, honestly.
Yeah, they'll be happy to hear it.
I'll make sure to mention it in the stand-up tomorrow.
It'll take a lot of the 'firefighting' off their plates.
Yeah, so, regarding the data pipeline, I think we're in a good spot to start looking for those specific skills.
It's going to be a heavy lift, but the team is ready for it.
Right. It's a priority.
We need that infrastructure solid before we can scale the next phase.
Exactly.
And speaking of scaling, we need to make sure the team doesn't get burnt out while we're waiting for those new hires to get up to speed.
That's why getting the new headcount integrated quickly is so vital.
Dana starts on the 14th, so please plan her first week.
Oh, okay. Right. I'll... um, I'll get a plan together.
I'll make sure she's not just sitting there waiting for tasks.
I want her to get into the codebase immediately, but, you know, in a way that doesn't overwhelm her.
Maybe start with some of the documentation updates first?
That sounds like a good starting point.
Just make sure she meets the core team early on.
Yeah, definitely. I'll set up some 1-on-1s with the senior devs.
It's important for her to feel... uh, welcomed.
Like she's part of the group right away.
I'll also make sure she has a clear roadmap for the first few weeks so she knows what the milestones are.
Good. We need her to feel productive as soon as possible.
Right. I'll handle that. I'll also...
um, I'll check if we have enough hardware ready.
I think we're good on the laptops, but I'll double-check the permissions for the dev environment.
Sometimes that's a bit of a headache with the security protocols.
Yeah, the permissions can be a pain.
Just make sure IT is looped in.
I'll reach out to them today. I'll get that sorted.
And, uh, I was thinking, maybe we can have her shadow a few of the stand-ups early on?
Just to get a feel for the workflow.
It helps a lot with the transition.
That's a great idea. Let's do that.
Okay, great.
So, I'll put together a draft of the onboarding schedule and send it over for you to look at.
I'll try to have that to you by the end of the day, just to make sure we're aligned on the goals for her first few weeks.
Perfect. That would be very helpful.
No problem. I'll get on that right after this call.
I'll also make sure the team knows she's coming so they can...
you know, be prepared to welcome her.
Mm-hmm. That's good.
Yeah. I'll keep you posted on the progress.
So, moving on to the actual sprint capacity...
I wanted to walk through how the team is feeling about the current workload.
Because, honestly, it's been pretty heavy since we shifted focus toward the Atlas push.
Yeah, I've noticed.
Some of the folks in the Slack channel mentioned it's been a bit of a grind.
Right, exactly.
And I think the main concern is that while the Atlas stuff is the priority, the day-to-day maintenance and the technical debt from the last cycle are still piling up.
It's like they're trying to run two different projects at once.
Is it manageable? I mean, for the next few weeks?
It's... well, it's manageable, but it's not sustainable.
If we keep pushing them at this pace, we're going to see some burnout by the time we actually hit the launch date.
I'm seeing some people staying late just to clear their tickets, and I'd rather they weren't doing that.
Okay. So what are you suggesting we do then?
I think we need to be more aggressive about what we're pushing to the next sprint.
Like, we need to identify the 'must-haves' for the immediate release and just...
move the 'nice-to-haves' out.
There are a few features in the backlog that we keep talking about, but they aren't critical for the initial rollout.
If we can cut those out, it gives the team some breathing room.
Mm-hmm. And that would help with the morale issue?
Yeah, definitely. It gives them a clear win.
Right now, the list is so long that it feels like they're never going to cross the finish line.
If we trim the scope, they can actually see progress.
I'd also like to, um, maybe carve out some time for just...
internal improvements. Not features, just making their own lives easier.
Like refactoring that one module that keeps breaking.
I see. And how much of a shift are we talking about?
Not a massive overhaul, but maybe about twenty percent of the current sprint capacity.
If we can just give them a little bit of space to breathe and focus on quality rather than just quantity, I think the energy levels will stabilize.
They're feeling a bit... I don't know, frazzled?
So, just a bit of a breather in the schedule would go a long way.
Okay, let's look at the backlog together then and see what we can move.
Yeah, that would be great.
I can pull up the list and we can just...
yeah, highlight the ones that aren't essential for the immediate launch.
So, looking at the sprint board, it's pretty clear that while the overall progress is good, we have a few specific people who are just...
they're hitting a wall.
I'm seeing some red flags on the capacity side.
Yeah, I've noticed that too.
It feels like a few people are carrying a lot of the heavy lifting for the core features.
Exactly. And the risk there is burnout, especially with the Atlas push.
If we keep pushing them at this pace, we're going to see some drop-offs in quality, or worse, people just getting exhausted.
I think we need to look at the tasks assigned to the backend team specifically.
Right, the backend. They've been grinding on the integration for weeks.
Mm-hmm.
And because they're so deep in the weeds, they haven't had a chance to breathe.
I'd like to move some of the non-critical documentation and the minor UI tweaks over to the frontend folks who have a bit more breathing room right now.
That makes sense.
Is the frontend team actually able to take that on without falling behind on their own tasks?
I think so. If we prioritize the high-impact items for them first.
We can push the minor stuff to the next cycle.
It's about balancing the load so no one is at 110% every single day.
Okay. So, how do we communicate that shift?
I don't want it to sound like we're just dumping more work on the frontend team.
I'll frame it as a strategic reallocation.
We're trying to protect the core team's focus on the critical path.
I'll talk to the lead on the frontend side first to make sure they're comfortable with the scope before we announce it to the whole group.
Good. That's a good way to put it.
Let's make sure we're actually moving those tickets over by the end of the week.
Yeah, I can do that.
I'll also check in with the new hire.
I want to make sure they aren't feeling overwhelmed by the onboarding process while also trying to contribute.
They're still getting their bearings.
Right, they're still new.
We don't want them feeling like they have to prove themselves by overworking.
Exactly. It's about sustainability.
If we can balance this out now, the push toward the beta will be much smoother.
It's better to slow down a little bit now than to have a total collapse right before the launch.
I agree. Let's try to get that rebalance done by Friday.
Perfect. I'll start on those conversations today.
So, moving on to the incident report from the weekend.
I've been digging through the logs to get a clear picture of what happened.
Yeah, I saw the Slack notifications pinging.
It seemed like it was a pretty quick resolution, but I want to know what actually triggered it.
Right.
Well, the outage on Saturday lasted 47 minutes from the first alert to the fix.
Okay. Forty-seven minutes. That's...
that's not too long, but I want to know why it took that long to identify the specific component.
Um, the initial alert was a bit generic.
It flagged a spike in latency, but it didn't immediately point to the database connection pool.
It took a few minutes for the on-call engineer to realize that the connection limit was being hit because of a new query.
A new query? Was that part of the latest deployment?
No, actually, it was a legacy query that started behaving differently because of a change in the underlying data structure.
It was...
uh, it was kind of a ghost in the machine, if that makes sense.
Right.
So it wasn't a direct result of the new code we pushed on Friday?
Exactly. It was a side effect.
The team had to manually scale the pool to get things moving, and then they had to find the specific query causing the leak.
And how was it actually found?
Like, did the automated monitoring catch the specific query or was it manual investigation?
It was a bit of both.
The monitoring caught the spike, but the identification of the specific query happened during the triage.
They had to look at the slow query logs to see what was hanging.
Mm-hmm.
And do we have a plan to make that alert more specific next time?
Yeah, that's the plan.
We're working on a more granular alert for the connection pool so that if it happens again, the team knows exactly where to look immediately.
We're also going to...
uh, we're going to add a check in the CI pipeline to flag any queries that don't meet our performance standards before they hit production.
That sounds like a solid way to prevent it from happening again.
I'm glad it was caught quickly.
Yeah, the team handled it well. They were very responsive.
Yeah, so, looking back at the outage, the main issue was that—uh—the connection pool wasn't scaling with the spike in traffic, and it just...
it just choked the whole service.
Right.
And was it the automated scaling that failed or was it a configuration error?
It was a bit of both, honestly.
The auto-scaling kicked in, but the configuration limit was set too low for the peak.
So, it stayed capped.
We caught it because the monitoring alerts fired, but by then, the latency was already spiking for everyone.
Okay. And the team's response time was pretty good, I think?
Mm-hmm, yeah. They jumped on it pretty quickly once the alerts hit.
We had to manually bump the limits and then restart the pods.
It took about...
uh, a little while to stabilize, but we got it back up.
Good.
We need to make sure that doesn't happen again during the Atlas launch.
Exactly.
We're already looking at the logs to see if there are any other bottlenecks.
We want to make sure the infrastructure is robust enough for the beta.
Can you write the postmortem by Friday?
Yes, I'll have the postmortem done by Friday.
Great.
I'd like to see the specific steps we're taking to automate that fix.
Yeah, I'll include that. We're planning to...
uh, implement a more dynamic threshold for the pool.
It's not just about fixing the immediate bug, but making sure the system handles the next spike automatically.
That makes sense. And the team's morale after the weekend?
They're a bit tired, yeah.
A bit of a grind over the weekend, but they're focused.
They actually liked the challenge of troubleshooting it, but they definitely want to move toward a more stable environment before the big push.
Right.
Well, let's just make sure we're clear on the technical debt we're accruing by skipping those checks.
I'm on it.
I'll have the team prioritize those specific patches in the next sprint.
We can't let the technical debt pile up too much before the beta goes live.
Good. Let's move on to the next item.
So, yeah, looking at the post-mortem from the weekend, the biggest takeaway is definitely the visibility gap.
We knew something was wrong, but we didn't know exactly where until the users started complaining on social media.
Right. It was like we were flying blind for about forty minutes.
Exactly. And that's the core issue.
We have basic heartbeats, but we don't have granular enough alerting on the downstream services.
So, the primary database was struggling, but the dashboard just showed a green light because the connection was technically still active, just...
uh, extremely slow.
So we need more granular metrics?
Yeah, but specifically for the latency thresholds.
We need to be alerted when a query takes longer than, say, two seconds, not just when it fails entirely.
Because in this case, it didn't fail, it just crawled.
And the system didn't know how to handle that backlog, so it just kept piling up.
Mm-hmm. And that's why the auto-scaling didn't kick in?
Precisely.
Because the load balancer didn't see a 'failure' signal, it didn't spin up new instances.
It just kept routing traffic to the struggling nodes.
So, we need to implement some circuit breakers there.
If a service is taking too long, we need to trip the breaker and, you know, serve a cached response or a 'busy' message instead of just letting the request hang.
Okay. That makes sense.
Is that something the team can prioritize this sprint?
I'd like to. I mean, I'd love to.
But, um, we have to balance that against the Atlas beta prep.
I'm thinking we can start with the most critical paths first.
Like, the authentication flow and the main dashboard.
We can't have those hanging.
We can probably push the less critical internal tools to the next sprint.
I agree. Let's focus on the high-traffic areas first.
Right. And another thing—the logging.
We realized that during the outage, the logs were actually there, but they were so voluminous that it was hard to parse them in real-time.
We need to move toward a more structured logging format so we can set up automated alerts for specific error codes.
Like, if we see a spike in 504s, we want a page to go out immediately, not just a notification in a Slack channel that someone might miss.
Good point. The Slack notifications are often buried.
Yeah, exactly. It's too easy to ignore.
We need a 'hard' alert for anything that impacts the end-user experience directly.
That's the main gap we need to close before the beta goes live.
So, yeah, looking at those gaps we just talked about, the main issue is that the system was technically 'up' but the processing layer was just...
it was just stalling.
The alerts didn't fire because the heartbeat was still active.
Right. It was a silent failure, basically.
Exactly. And that's what we need to fix for the next one.
We need to move away from just checking if the service is alive and start checking if the data is actually moving.
I'm thinking we should implement some threshold-based alerts on the queue depth.
Okay, but how do we do that without getting flooded with notifications every five minutes?
Um, well, that's the thing. We can set a baseline.
Like, if the queue grows by more than, uh, a certain percentage in a ten-minute window, then it triggers a high-priority page.
It won't be for every tiny blip, but it'll catch the stall before it becomes a full-blown outage.
That makes sense. I like that approach.
Yeah. And I also want to look at the notification routing.
Right now, it goes to a general channel where it's easy to miss.
I'd like to route these specific infrastructure alerts to a dedicated on-call rotation group so someone is actually looking at it the second it pops.
Is the team on board with that?
I don't want them feeling like they're being nagged.
I think they'd actually prefer it.
They're tired of finding out about issues from users on social media instead of from our own tools.
It's a lot less stressful to get a ping early than to spend three hours in a war room trying to figure out what happened.
Fair point. So, what's the timeline for getting those new thresholds in?
I can have the team map out the specific thresholds by the end of the week.
We can probably have the first set of alerts live by the next sprint.
It's not a massive overhaul, just...
just some targeted tweaks to the monitoring logic.
Okay. Let's do that.
And let's make sure we document the new logic so we don't forget why we set those specific numbers.
Oh, definitely. I'll make sure the wiki is updated.
We need to be able to explain why we chose these specific triggers if we ever have to revisit them.
Mm-hmm. Good. Let's move on to the next item.
Yeah, so, moving on to the infrastructure side of things, specifically the tooling.
